warmup.q: Each server counts a card's attempts in Redis with two separate commands. First, "add one to this card's counter". Then, only if the counter is now 1, "delete this counter in 60 seconds". Attempts are refused once the counter passes 5. A server crashes right after the first command returned 1. What happens to the card?
options: Nothing: Redis deletes the counter after 60 seconds anyway
The counter never gets its 60-second deadline, so after a few more attempts the card is refused for good
The next attempt sees 2 and sets the missing deadline
Redis undoes the add, because the server that sent it crashed
warmup.why: Only the attempt that saw 1 would set the deadline, and that server died. Every later attempt sees 2, 3, 4 and skips it, so the counter never gets one and never starts over. Redis has nothing to undo: the add was a complete command, and the deadline command was never sent. The first section of this lesson builds this limit, breaks it this way, and fixes it.

sections.h: One shared counter per card, with a deadline
sections.html:
Let's start with the thief. Card testing looks like this: one stolen card number, 300 attempts in a minute, each with a different security code (the three digits on the back), until one is approved. The rule that stops it is plain: at most 5 attempts per card per minute. A rule that caps how often something may happen is a rate limit. The question is where the count lives.

The simplest version keeps a counter per card in each server's memory. It breaks as soon as there are 20 servers behind a load balancer, a program that hands each incoming request to one of the servers. Each server allows 5, so the card gets 100 attempts a minute. The count has to be shared, and Redis can hold it. INCR rl:card:7 adds one to the number stored under the key rl:card:7 (rate limit, card 7) and returns the new value. Redis runs one command at a time, on a single line of work called a thread (Inside an in-memory store: how Redis executes commands). So 20 servers calling INCR at once never lose an increment.

The count must also start over every minute. That's a fixed window: the minute is the window, and the counter resets when it ends. Let the first attempt of the window give the key a TTL (time to live) of 60 seconds. That's a deadline after which Redis deletes the key by itself (Expiry, eviction and memory). Here it is in Java and in Kotlin. redis is a connection made with Jedis, the Java library the labs use to talk to Redis:

Java
long n = redis.incr("rl:card:7");
if (n == 1) redis.expire("rl:card:7", 60);     // the first attempt of the window starts the clock
boolean allowed = n <= 5;
Kotlin
val n = redis.incr("rl:card:7")
if (n == 1L) redis.expire("rl:card:7", 60)     // the first attempt of the window starts the clock
val allowed = n <= 5

Kotlin writes 1L because incr returns a Long, a 64-bit whole number, and Kotlin won't compare it with a plain 1.

This works until a server dies between the two commands. Say it crashes, or its connection drops, right after the INCR that returned 1. Now rl:card:7 holds 1 and has no TTL. The next attempt gets 2, so it doesn't set the TTL, and neither does any attempt after it. The counter never resets, and from the sixth attempt on, card 7 is refused for good, thief or owner. One command runs alone, but a sequence of commands doesn't, and a sequence can stop halfway.

The fix is to make it one command. EVAL runs a script, a small program in the Lua language, as one command, so a script can run INCR and EXPIRE together. The Try it below has one. Redis 8.8 added a built-in command for exactly this job: INCREX rl:card:7 BYINT 1 UBOUND 5 EX 60 ENX. It adds one unless that would pass 5, and sets a 60-second TTL in the same command. ENX means "set the TTL only if the key has none yet". Without it, every attempt that gets in restarts the 60 seconds, and the window stretches. The reply is two numbers, the new value and the amount actually added, so [5, 0] means refused.

That's the model for this lesson. For every request, each server asks Redis one question: "may this go ahead?" Redis must answer and record the answer in one command, with a deadline on the record so that it cleans itself up. The rest of the lesson changes what the record holds, ending with a payment's stored answer. First, though, the fixed window has a seam.

try.title: Leak a counter, then fix it two ways
steps: Start Redis from the labs folder if it isn't running (docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d), and open its prompt: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli. Docker runs Redis in a container, a sealed-off box on your laptop, and redis-cli is the program you type Redis commands into.

The first line clears anything an earlier run left. Run the next five commands, and pretend your server died between its INCR and its EXPIRE, so the EXPIRE is never sent. Lines that start with # are notes, so skip them. Read both TTL answers.
Run the script, then INCREX six times. Predict the sixth reply before you send it.

Two more INCRs print 2 and 3, and the TTL is still -1. Nothing will ever set it. After DEL, the script prints (integer) 1 and TTL prints (integer) 60: the same command set it. The first five INCREX calls print 1) (integer) 1 and 2) (integer) 1, up to 1) (integer) 5 and 2) (integer) 1. The sixth prints 1) (integer) 5 and 2) (integer) 0: refused, and the counter stays at 5. The last TTL is 60, or 59 if a second ticked over.

sections.h: A sliding window remembers when each attempt happened
sections.html:
A fixed window has a seam at every minute boundary. Five attempts between 0:59.0 and 0:59.4 fill minute 0. Five more between 1:00.0 and 1:00.4 fill minute 1, which started empty. The limit said 5 a minute, and the card got 10 in 1.4 seconds.

What the rule means is "at most 5 in any 60 seconds, counted back from now". Picture a frame 60 seconds wide that slides along with the clock. That's a sliding window. Counting inside it needs the time of each recent attempt, so the record becomes a log: one entry, with its time, for each attempt that got in.

Redis's sorted set fits (Core data types and their encodings). It's a set of members, each with a number called its score, kept in order of score. Here each member is one attempt with a unique id, and its score is the time in milliseconds. Because members stay in order, dropping the old ones takes one command. For an attempt at time now:

  1. ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rl:card:7 -inf <now - 60000> drops every attempt that's 60 seconds old or older.
  2. ZCARD rl:card:7 counts what's left.
  3. Fewer than 5: ZADD rl:card:7 <now> <id> and PEXPIRE rl:card:7 60000 (a TTL in milliseconds), then let the attempt in. Otherwise, refuse it and record nothing. If you recorded refusals, a card that kept trying would never get back under the limit.

Sent as separate commands, this is check-then-act: a decision made on a read that's out of date by the time you act on it. Two servers both run ZCARD, both read 4, both ZADD, and 6 attempts get in. In the demo, 32 threads each sent one attempt at the same instant. The separate commands let in anywhere from 5 to 18, a different number on most runs. The same steps in one Lua script let in exactly 5, every time. The lab's SlidingWindowLimiter is that script. Use a random id as the member, such as a UUID (a random 128-bit number that practically never repeats), not the time. Two attempts in the same millisecond would otherwise share one member and count as one.

The price is memory: one member per attempt that got in. A limit of 5 per minute costs 5 members per card, but 10,000 per hour per shop costs 10,000. When that's too much, estimate. The sliding window counter keeps two fixed-window counts, this minute's and last minute's. It weights the old count by how much of last minute still lies inside the past 60 seconds. Cloudflare, a company whose computers sit in front of millions of websites, gives an example. The limit is 50 a minute, last minute had 42 requests, and the minute that began 15 seconds ago has 18 so far. The last 45 seconds of last minute are still inside the window, so the estimate is 42 × 45/60 + 18 = 49.5, under the limit.

The estimate assumes last minute's requests were spread evenly. Cloudflare measured what that costs on 400 million requests from 270,000 sources: 0.003% of requests were wrongly allowed or limited, and the estimate was 6% off the real rate on average. And it costs two whole numbers per card, whatever the limit.

Both windows treat every second alike. Some honest programs don't send that way, and next we'll make room for them.

sections.h: A token bucket, or GCRA, allows a burst and then a steady rate
sections.html:
Some honest programs send in bursts. Picture a shop's program that sends the hour's refunds all at once: 40 requests in one second at the end of every hour, and nothing in between. A limit of 5 per minute refuses most of that burst. A limit of 40 per second lets a broken program send 40 every second, forever. What you want is "a burst of up to 10, then 2 per second on average".

That's a token bucket. Picture a jar on a counter that holds at most 10 tokens and gains one token every 500 ms. Each request takes a token, or is refused if the jar is empty. A program that was quiet finds a full jar and can spend all 10 at once. After that, it gets one request per new token: 2 a second.

You don't need a timer that drops tokens into the jar. Store two numbers per client, the program sending the requests, in a Redis hash: a small table of named fields under one key. tokens is how many were left after its last request, and ts is when the jar was last topped up. On each request, work out how many tokens it has earned since ts, add them (never above 10) and take one. Do it all in one script, so that two servers never both take the last token. The worked example builds it. The key's TTL is the time the jar takes to fill from empty: after 5 quiet seconds the jar would be full anyway, so Redis may forget it.

GCRA, the generic cell rate algorithm, gives the same answers with one number. It comes from ATM, an old network technology for telephone companies (nothing to do with cash machines). Instead of counting tokens, it keeps a schedule: the theoretical arrival time (TAT), when this client's next request would be due if it sent at exactly the allowed rate. Each request that gets in pushes the TAT one interval later, 500 ms here. A request is refused if it would push the TAT more than 10 intervals past now, the size of the burst. A quiet client's TAT falls behind the clock and counts as now, which is the same as a full jar. Nothing ever has to top up tokens in the background. The demo below sends the same requests to both, and they agree on every one.

So which one should you use? A fixed window with INCREX is one key and one command, but its seam lets up to twice the limit through: fine for rough limits against abuse, such as 1,000 requests a minute from one internet address. The sliding log is exact and costs one member per request, so it suits small limits such as attempts per card. The sliding window counter is the cheap estimate for big limits. A token bucket or GCRA suits a cap on how often a customer's program may call your service.

Every limiter so far stops a request that comes too often, and the thief is handled. The customer who pressed Pay twice isn't a thief, though, and a limit of 5 lets both presses through. Next, we'll learn to recognize a repeat.

steps: Run TokenBucketDemo or TokenBucketDemoKt from the labs folder. It sends the same requests to a token bucket and to GCRA, both set to a burst of 10 and one request per 500 ms. The demo uses a made-up clock, so the output is the same on every run.

code.title: TokenBucketDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.cache.l08.demo; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import java.util.List; /** A token bucket and GCRA in Lua: a burst of 10, then one request every 500 ms. The same traffic for both. */ public class TokenBucketDemo { // KEYS[1] the bucket (a hash with tokens and ts). ARGV[1] capacity, ARGV[2] ms per new token, ARGV[3] now in ms. static final String TOKEN_BUCKET = """ local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1]) local interval = tonumber(ARGV[2]) local now = tonumber(ARGV[3]) local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts') local tokens, ts = tonumber(b[1]), tonumber(b[2]) if tokens == nil then -- a bucket nobody used yet starts full tokens, ts = capacity, now end local earned = math.floor((now - ts) / interval) -- whole tokens since ts if earned > 0 then tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + earned) ts = ts + earned * interval -- keep the part of a token not earned yet end local allowed = 0 if tokens > 0 then tokens = tokens - 1 allowed = 1 end redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', ts) redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], capacity * interval) -- idle that long, it is full again: forget it return allowed """; // KEYS[1] the theoretical arrival time (TAT) in ms. ARGV[1] burst, ARGV[2] ms per request, ARGV[3] now in ms. static final String GCRA = """ local burst = tonumber(ARGV[1]) local interval = tonumber(ARGV[2]) local now = tonumber(ARGV[3]) local tat = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])) or now if tat < now then tat = now end -- a quiet client: its schedule restarts now local next = tat + interval -- where this request would push the schedule if next - now > burst * interval then return 0 end -- too far ahead of the allowed rate redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], next, 'PX', next - now) -- once the clock catches up, forget it return 1 """; static final String BUCKET_KEY = "demo:l08:bucket:merchant:m-17"; static final String GCRA_KEY = "demo:l08:gcra:merchant:m-17"; interface Limiter { boolean take(long now); } static void run(String label, Limiter limiter) { long t0 = 1_762_500_000_000L; // a pretend clock, passed in, so every run is the same int burst = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 15; i++) if (limiter.take(t0)) burst++; StringBuilder line = new StringBuilder(); int steady = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) { boolean ok = limiter.take(t0 + i * 250L); if (ok) steady++; line.append(ok ? '+' : '.'); } int afterRest = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 15; i++) if (limiter.take(t0 + 10_000)) afterRest++; System.out.printf("%-13s burst of 15 at t = 0: %2d every 250 ms for 5 s: %2d of 20 %s burst after 5 quiet s: %2d%n", label, burst, steady, line, afterRest); } public static void main(String[] args) { try (RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build()) { redis.del(BUCKET_KEY, GCRA_KEY); run("token bucket", now -> Long.valueOf(1).equals( redis.eval(TOKEN_BUCKET, List.of(BUCKET_KEY), List.of("10", "500", String.valueOf(now))))); run("GCRA", now -> Long.valueOf(1).equals( redis.eval(GCRA, List.of(GCRA_KEY), List.of("10", "500", String.valueOf(now))))); System.out.println("token bucket state: " + redis.hgetAll(BUCKET_KEY) + ", PTTL " + redis.pttl(BUCKET_KEY) + " ms"); System.out.println("GCRA state: " + redis.get(GCRA_KEY) + ", PTTL " + redis.pttl(GCRA_KEY) + " ms"); } } }

sections.h: Recognizing a payment sent twice: the idempotency key
sections.html:
Here's the Pay button from the program's side. The checkout program, the client, sends the payment to one of the company's servers, which asks the card's bank to approve it. The bank takes 120 ms. But the checkout program waits at most 100 ms for an answer, its timeout. So it gives up and sends the payment again, and another server charges the card a second time. Nothing was broken. Sending again, a retry, is how programs survive a network that sometimes loses messages, and a client that gives up can't tell whether its request or only the answer was lost.

So the server has to recognize a retry. Picture ordering a book by post. You fill in the form, write an order number of your own at the top, say 7f3a, and post it. Weeks pass with no reply, so you post a copy with the same number. The shop files every reply it sends in a drawer, by order number. When your copy arrives, the clerk finds 7f3a in the drawer and posts you a copy of the same reply, and no second book.

Programs do the same. The client makes up one number per payment, usually a UUID, and sends it with every attempt in a header named Idempotency-Key. (A header is a labelled line sent in front of a request on the web.) The server stores its answer to the first attempt under that number, and answers every retry with the stored answer instead of doing the work again. The number is an idempotency key. Idempotent is a word from mathematics for an action that has the same effect whether you do it once or ten times. The key makes a payment work that way: every attempt after the first changes nothing.

Stripe, a company whose service lets shops take card payments, works like this. It saves the status code and body of its first answer, and keeps keys for at least 24 hours. (Every answer on the web starts with a three-digit status code: 200 means OK.) The IETF, the group that writes the internet's standards, has a draft standard for the header, at version 08.

The simplest version reuses the cache pattern from Caching patterns and stampedes: GET idem:k-7f3a, return the stored answer if it's there, otherwise charge and SET the answer. It breaks when two copies of the same request are in flight at once, and that's exactly the timeout case. The retry arrives while the first attempt still waits for the bank. Both GETs find nothing, and both servers charge. It's check-then-act again.

So claim the key before doing the work, in one command, the way the book shop's clerk pins up a note, "7f3a: being handled", before she packs anything. SET idem:k-7f3a <pending> NX PX 30000 succeeds for exactly one request, because NX stores only if the key doesn't exist yet. Add GET, and the same command also tells the loser what's there. SET key value NX GET (allowed since Redis 7.0) returns nil when it stored your value, and the existing value, unchanged, when it didn't. That's one trip to Redis, with no gap between "is it there?" and "it's mine".

While the first attempt works, the value says PENDING. When the charge returns, the server replaces it with DONE plus the exact answer, with a TTL of 24 hours. A retry that finds PENDING gets 409 Conflict, meaning "try again shortly". A retry that finds DONE gets the stored answer, byte for byte. The stepper plays the whole timeout case.

That's where the book shop picture breaks: a real shop keeps its drawer for years, but Redis forgets each key when its TTL runs out, and a later retry looks new. Next, we'll see what else the record needs.

try.title: Claim a key, collide with a retry, replay the answer
steps: At a redis-cli prompt (docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli), run the DEL, which clears an earlier run, and the first two SETs. The second plays the retry: same key, same body fingerprint, a new attempt token.
Finish the first attempt with the XX SET, which writes only if the key exists. Its value holds the answer in JSON, a common text format for data. Then send a third attempt, and predict its reply.
Read the TTL. How long will this key answer retries?

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
DEL idem:k-7f3a
SET idem:k-7f3a P|h-4f1c|t-1 NX GET PX 30000
SET idem:k-7f3a P|h-4f1c|t-2 NX GET PX 30000
PTTL idem:k-7f3a
SET idem:k-7f3a 'D|h-4f1c|{"payment":"p-981","status":"approved"}' XX PX 86400000
SET idem:k-7f3a P|h-4f1c|t-3 NX GET PX 30000
TTL idem:k-7f3a

try.expect: The first DEL prints (integer) 0, or 1 if an earlier run left the key behind. The first SET prints (nil): the key was free, and attempt t-1 owns it now. The second prints "P|h-4f1c|t-1": NX refused, and GET showed a PENDING with the same fingerprint, so this retry should get 409. PTTL, the time left in milliseconds, is just under 30000. The XX SET prints OK. The third attempt prints "D|h-4f1c|{\"payment\":\"p-981\",\"status\":\"approved\"}" (redis-cli escapes the inner quotes): DONE with the same fingerprint, so the server sends that body back. TTL prints (integer) 86400: retries are answered for a day.

refs.title: SET: NX, GET and the IFEQ conditions

sections.h: The record needs a fingerprint, a deadline and an owner
sections.html:
Three things go wrong with a record that only says PENDING or DONE, and each one adds a part to it.

The first is a key reused for a different payment. A bug in the client sends a 40-euro payment with the key of yesterday's 12.50-euro payment. The server finds DONE and replays "approved, 12.50". The client believes the 40 euros were paid, and nothing was charged. So the record stores a fingerprint of the request, called a hash. (It's a different thing from Redis's hash type: a short value worked out from the request's bytes. The same bytes always give the same hash, and different bytes almost never do.) A request whose hash differs gets 422 Unprocessable Content. The IETF draft asks for these status codes: 409 while the first request is still being processed, and 422 for a key reused with a different body. In the book shop, the clerk checks that the copy asks for the same book before she sends the old reply.

The second is a server that dies while its record says PENDING. Every retry then gets 409, forever. So PENDING gets its own short TTL, longer than the slowest attempt can take. If the bank's answer never takes more than 10 seconds, 30 seconds is enough. After that, a retry can claim the key again.

That TTL creates the third problem. Attempt 1 is slow, and its PENDING runs out. The retry, attempt 2, claims the key and starts. Then attempt 1 comes back from the bank with a decline and writes DONE over attempt 2's record. Attempt 2 is approved and writes its DONE too, or it finishes first and attempt 1 overwrites it. Either way, the stored answer may not match what happened last. So PENDING carries a random token for its attempt, P|<hash>|<token>, and finishing is a compare-and-set: write DONE only if the key still holds exactly this attempt's PENDING. On Redis 8.4 and later, SET key <done> IFEQ <my pending> PX 86400000 does it in one command; before 8.4 it's a three-line Lua script. A stale attempt's write changes nothing. The lab's IdempotencyStore is this record.

One gap is left, and Redis can't close it alone. If a server charges the card and dies before writing DONE, its PENDING runs out, and the next retry charges again. Redis can't know that the charge happened; only the system that moved the money can. So close the gap there. Send the same key to the payment provider, the outside company that talks to the banks, if it accepts one, as Stripe does. Or write the record in the same database transaction as the payment itself: a group of changes that the database saves all together or not at all.

Redis can spot a retry, but only the payment itself can refuse a second charge. Give the key to both.

That's also the limit of every record in this lesson: it lives only in Redis's memory. A forgotten rate limit lets a thief start over, and a forgotten idempotency key lets a retry charge twice.

try.title: Refuse a stale attempt and a reused key
steps: Clear the key, then claim k-9c01 as attempt t-1. Then DEL it again, which plays the 30-second PENDING TTL running out while attempt 1 is stuck waiting for the bank.
Let the retry, t-2, claim the key. Now play attempt 1 coming back late with a decline, then attempt 2 finishing with an approval. Predict both replies.
Last, send the same key with a different body fingerprint, h-9b20.

DEL idem:k-9c01
SET idem:k-9c01 P|h-4f1c|t-1 NX GET PX 30000
# 30 s pass: attempt t-1's PENDING expires
DEL idem:k-9c01
SET idem:k-9c01 P|h-4f1c|t-2 NX GET PX 30000

IFEQ P|h-4f1c|t-1 prints (nil): the key holds t-2's PENDING, so the stale decline is refused. Attempt 2's prints OK. The last SET prints "D|h-4f1c|{\"status\":\"approved\"}". The stored fingerprint is h-4f1c and this request's is h-9b20, so the server answers 422 and must not replay the approval.

refs.title: The Idempotency-Key HTTP header field (IETF draft)

opening:
Picture paying for concert tickets on your phone. You press Pay, and a little wheel spins. Did it work? You press Pay again. A payments program has received the same payment twice, and must decide whether to charge your card twice.

The same program has another visitor that minute: a thief with a stolen card number, trying it 300 times with a different security code each time.

The tempting fix for both is for the program to remember what it has seen. That works while one computer runs it. The company runs it on twenty computers, called servers, and each one sees only its own share.

In Keeping a cache honest, we used Redis, a program that keeps data in memory and answers many programs at once, as a copy of the database. Now it holds records that live nowhere else. In this lesson, we'll build a limit on attempts per card and find where it breaks. Then we'll build the record that recognizes a payment sent twice. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a Pay button pressed twice and a thief guessing codes. Both came down to one question that every server asks Redis, answered and recorded in one command. The thief meets a counter with a deadline. A second press, sent with the same idempotency key, meets the stored answer to the first.

If you write programs, open the developer documentation of a payment service, such as Stripe's, and search for "idempotency". You'll find the header from this lesson, and how long a key lasts.

Next, we'll ask what Redis loses when it restarts, since these records live only in its memory, and how it keeps a copy safe.

compare.title: An idempotent charge handler in Java and Kotlin

java.title: ChargeHandler.java
java.html: record Reply(int status, String body) {} // POST /payments: the Idempotency-Key header and the raw JSON body Reply charge(String idemKey, String requestJson) { String hash = sha256(requestJson); // same body, same hash IdempotencyStore.Begin begin = store.begin(idemKey, hash); if (begin instanceof IdempotencyStore.Begin.Replay replay) return new Reply(200, replay.getResponse()); if (begin instanceof IdempotencyStore.Begin.InProgress) return new Reply(409, "{\"error\":\"in progress\"}"); if (begin instanceof IdempotencyStore.Begin.Mismatch) return new Reply(422, "{\"error\":\"key reused\"}"); IdempotencyStore.Begin.Started started = (IdempotencyStore.Begin.Started) begin; String response = issuer.authorize(requestJson); // the side effect, once per key store.complete(idemKey, hash, started.getToken(), response); return new Reply(200, response); }

kotlin.title: ChargeHandler.kt
kotlin.html: data class Reply(val status: Int, val body: String) // POST /payments: the Idempotency-Key header and the raw JSON body fun charge(idemKey: String, requestJson: String): Reply { val hash = sha256(requestJson) // same body, same hash return when (val begin = store.begin(idemKey, hash)) { is Begin.Replay -> Reply(200, begin.response) Begin.InProgress -> Reply(409, """{"error":"in progress"}""") Begin.Mismatch -> Reply(422, """{"error":"key reused"}""") is Begin.Started -> { val response = issuer.authorize(requestJson) // the side effect, once per key store.complete(idemKey, hash, begin.token, response) Reply(200, response) } } }

compare.note: Both handlers call the lab's Kotlin IdempotencyStore, and send Redis the same commands: one SET ... NX GET before the charge and one SET ... IFEQ after it. They differ in how they handle the four outcomes. Kotlin's when over the sealed Begin interface, a type whose every kind is known in advance, is checked by the compiler: add a fifth outcome and this function stops compiling until you handle it. Java sees the Kotlin data objects as classes with a single instance, so it tests them with instanceof, and nothing warns you when a case is missing. A Java version of the store could declare Begin as a sealed interface of records, and use a pattern-matching switch to get the same check. Neither handler stores the reply's status code. A real one would keep it next to the body, so that a replay of a refusal returns the same status too.

worked.title: A token bucket in one Lua script

steps.say: Start with the state. A bucket is a hash with two fields: tokens, what was left after the last request, and ts, when the bucket was last topped up, in milliseconds. HMGET reads both in one call. Missing fields come back as false, which tonumber turns into nil, Lua's word for nothing. A bucket nobody has used yet starts full.
steps.code:
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local interval = tonumber(ARGV[2])     -- ms per new token: 500 means 2 per second
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens, ts = tonumber(b[1]), tonumber(b[2])
if tokens == nil then                  -- a new bucket starts full
    tokens, ts = capacity, now
end

steps.say: Top up without a timer. Count the whole tokens earned since ts, add them up to the capacity, and move ts forward by exactly those intervals. The leftover part of an interval stays in ts for the next request, so 250 ms plus 250 ms still earns a token, and whole-number arithmetic never drifts.
steps.code:
local earned = math.floor((now - ts) / interval)
if earned > 0 then
    tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + earned)
    ts = ts + earned * interval
end

steps.say: Take one token or refuse, write both fields back, and set the TTL to the time a bucket takes to fill from empty. A bucket that has been quiet that long is full again, so forgetting it changes no answer.
steps.code:
local allowed = 0
if tokens > 0 then
    tokens = tokens - 1
    allowed = 1
end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', ts)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], capacity * interval)
return allowed

steps.say: Call it with the bucket's key and three arguments. The script's 1 or 0 arrives in Java as a Long. This is the demo's call: 10 tokens, one every 500 ms, and the caller's clock.
steps.code: boolean take(String merchant, long nowMillis) { Object r = redis.eval(TOKEN_BUCKET, List.of("bucket:" + merchant), List.of("10", "500", String.valueOf(nowMillis))); return Long.valueOf(1).equals(r); }

alt.html: fun take(merchant: String, nowMillis: Long): Boolean = redis.eval(TOKEN_BUCKET, listOf("bucket:$merchant"), listOf("10", "500", nowMillis.toString())) == 1L

steps.say: Pick the clock last. Passing now in makes the script easy to test and its output the same on every run. NTP, the service that sets computers' clocks over the network, keeps servers within milliseconds of each other. If the servers' clocks can't be trusted, read Redis's own clock inside the script instead: local t = redis.call('TIME') returns seconds and microseconds, so now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000). Since Redis 7.0, a script may read TIME and still write. Copies of Redis on other machines, called replicas, receive the script's writes instead of running it again. Persistence and replication, the next lesson, meets replicas, and Serial execution: Redis MULTI, WATCH and Lua explains the rule.

drill.title: The fixed-window limiter from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write allow(card) for 5 attempts per card per 60 seconds as one Lua script, called through Jedis: INCR, set the TTL only on the first attempt, and return the count. Then name the Redis 8.8 command that replaces the script, with its options.

answer.html: static final String FIXED_WINDOW = """ local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]) if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end return n """; boolean allow(String card) { long n = (Long) redis.eval(FIXED_WINDOW, List.of("rl:" + card), List.of("60")); // one command: never TTL-less return n <= 5; } // Redis 8.8: INCREX rl:<card> BYINT 1 UBOUND 5 EX 60 ENX; allowed when the applied increment (2nd reply) is 1

alt.html: val FIXED_WINDOW = """ local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]) if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end return n """.trimIndent() fun allow(card: String): Boolean { val n = redis.eval(FIXED_WINDOW, listOf("rl:$card"), listOf("60")) as Long // one command: never TTL-less return n <= 5 } // Redis 8.8: INCREX rl:<card> BYINT 1 UBOUND 5 EX 60 ENX; allowed when the applied increment (2nd reply) is 1

recap: A limiter's check and its record must be one command. INCR and EXPIRE sent as two commands can leave a counter with no deadline, which never starts over.
A Lua script, or INCREX ... EX 60 ENX on Redis 8.8, fixes the fixed window. Even then, up to twice the limit gets through where two minutes meet.

A sliding window log is a sorted set of times that one script trims, counts and adds to: exact, at one member per request. The sliding window counter estimates it with two counts (Cloudflare: 0.003% wrong decisions).
A token bucket stores two numbers per client and allows a burst up to its size, then a steady rate. GCRA gives the same answers with one number, a schedule.
An idempotency key is claimed with SET ... NX GET before the work. PENDING holds a fingerprint of the request, an owner token and a short TTL; DONE holds the exact answer for 24 hours.

The limit: these records live only in Redis's memory, and a server that charges and dies before DONE still needs the payment provider's own idempotency, or the database transaction, to stop a second charge.

explain.prompt: A teammate proposes: GET idem:<key>, charge the card if nothing is there, then SET idem:<key> <answer> EX 86400. Explain what goes wrong, and what the record needs instead.
explain.answer: Two copies of the same payment are often in flight at once. The client gives up after 100 ms and retries while the first attempt still waits for the bank. Both GETs find nothing, and both servers charge. The check and the claim have to be one command, so the record is written before the charge: SET key PENDING NX GET PX 30000 stores it for exactly one request, and tells every other request what's there. Then the record needs more than a state. It needs a fingerprint of the body, so a key reused for another payment gets 422 instead of somebody else's answer. It needs a short TTL on PENDING, so a crashed server doesn't block the key forever. And it needs a random owner token, so a slow attempt that comes back after its PENDING ran out can't overwrite the new owner's record; finishing is SET ... IFEQ <my pending>. DONE holds the exact answer for 24 hours, and retries get it back byte for byte. A server that charges and dies before DONE still leaves a gap, which the payment provider's own idempotency key or the database transaction has to close.

deeper.html:
Where the limiter runs. A limit kept in Redis costs one trip over the network per request, about 0.2 ms on the lab laptop (Inside an in-memory store: how Redis executes commands). If a limit only protects your own service from too much traffic, a limiter inside each server needs no network at all, such as the one in Resilience4j, a Java library of tools like this. Set it to the total divided by the number of servers. It drifts when the number of servers changes. Limits that are business rules, such as attempts per card, need the shared count.

Choosing the idempotency key. The key must be the same on every retry of one payment, and different for different payments. For a program calling a web service, that's a UUID made once per payment and kept across retries. For a program reading from Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages for others to read, it's the payment id, or the message's place in the log (its topic, partition and offset). For a workflow engine such as Temporal, which retries steps for you, it's the workflow's id plus the step's id. A fresh UUID per attempt is the classic mistake: every retry looks new.

Storing the status code. The lab stores only the answer's body. A real record also keeps the status code and any headers the client depends on, so that a replay of a refusal, such as a 402 (payment required) or a 422, is the same answer as the original.

Redis Cluster. Every script here touches one key, so limiter and idempotency keys spread across the machines of a Redis Cluster without hash tags, the curly braces in names like merchant:{m-17} (Redis Cluster and production operations).

INCREX for the counter. The sliding window counter needs two counters per card, each with a TTL of two windows. Redis 8.8's INCREX ... EX 120 ENX adds to the current one and sets its TTL in one command, and a GET of the previous one completes the estimate. Cloudflare's version did the same with one INCR and one GET.

More on the estimates. In Cloudflare's measurement, the only sources the sliding window counter got wrong were 3 that it let through at less than 15% over their limit. Brandur Leach's 2015 write-up on GCRA names the background job that tops up tokens as the great weakness of the leaky bucket, an older design that GCRA does without.

Ready-made limiters. If you'd rather not write Lua, Redisson, another Java library for Redis, keeps a limiter in Redis for you: trySetRate(RateType.OVERALL, 2, Duration.ofSeconds(1)), then tryAcquire(). Its documentation says it doesn't guarantee fairness. The Encoding, APIs and workflows track, later in this part, comes back to how idempotency keys travel between programs.
